title: Guardian: The Security Watchdog That Lives Outside the Vault
excerpt: Someone planted sleeping malware in my code — disguised as fonts and editor settings, delivered through commits that looked exactly like mine. Here is why the answer was a watchdog that lives outside my repositories, and what that taught me about trust.
author: Athalla Rizky
body:
## Commits That Looked Like Mine

In October 2026, a routine look at my own repositories surfaced something unsettling: commits that carried **my commit messages, my dates, my author names** — but I never made them. Someone had rewritten history underneath me, planting foreign material inside lookalike commits designed to survive a casual glance.

This is a real attack class, and it has a name: a **supply-chain campaign**. The idea isn't to break into your computer with a bang. It's to slip quiet things into the places you already trust — your own code — and wait.

## What Was Actually Planted

To be clear about the threat without the jargon, here is what the campaign plants, translated:

- **A trap wired to your editor's door.** A tiny configuration file that makes your code editor run a task *the moment you open the folder*. You don't click anything. Opening the project is the trigger.
- **Fake fonts that are actually code.** Files named like innocent font assets — but they're text in disguise, waiting to fetch and run worse things from the internet.
- **Riders on your build.** Small additions to existing config files, so the payload also wakes up when you normally build or develop the project.

Everything is **dormant** and everything is **camouflaged**. The font files are genuinely real fonts on the outside. The editor files are inert-looking settings. Each piece alone can talk its way past a guard. It's the *combination* — and the fact that a fonts folder appeared overnight in projects that never had one — that gives the campaign away.

## Why You Can't Guard the Vault with the Thief's Key

My first instinct was the obvious one: add protection *inside* the repositories. A check, a script, a rule.

Then the flaw hits you. **The same stolen key that let the attacker in can also switch off anything stored inside.** Workflows, protections, revert scripts — they're all just files in the repo. A lock inside the vault is only as trustworthy as the vault's least trustworthy keyholder.

That one insight shaped everything that followed: **the watcher has to live outside the blast radius.**

## What Guardian Is

[Guardian](https://github.com/athallarizky/guardian) is my answer: a security guard that lives in its own separate place and **walks around every project I own, on a schedule, looking for the fingerprints of exactly this campaign** — the editor trap, the fake-font folder, the config riders, the loader strings.

When it finds something, two things happen: it **files a report** (a ticket, so nothing gets lost), and it **pings my phone** — a Telegram alert naming the actual repositories involved. No vague warnings; real names, immediately.

And by design, the intruder cannot silence it. Guardian's credential can only **read**. There is nothing it can edit, disable, or delete — including Guardian's own alarms.

## The Alarm Clock Needed Its Own Alarm Clock

Reality added a chapter no plan predicted. After the campaign, GitHub's own scheduler started *silently* skipping Guardian's hourly check — the runs just didn't happen, with no error anywhere. (Working as intended: protections get noisy around abuse-flagged accounts.)

The fix was almost comedic: a tiny independent heartbeat on Cloudflare that checks "did Guardian actually run recently?" — and re-triggers it if the schedule went quiet. A backup alarm clock for the alarm clock. It cost nothing, it lives on a third platform, and it coexists peacefully with the original schedule: whoever fires first wins, and nothing runs twice.

## Three Lessons Worth Keeping

- **Camouflage beats "looks suspicious."** The planted fonts were real fonts; the settings were valid JSON. Detection that asks *"does this file look evil?"* loses. Detection that asks *"why does a fonts folder exist in a project that never had one?"* wins. Presence and placement, not appearance.
- **Controls must live outside the blast radius.** Any protection that the attacking credential can edit is not a protection — it's decoration.
- **Silence is not safety.** Early on, a throttled run failed its lookups and reported everything as clean. Since then, every failure is a loud ERROR, never a green checkmark. A check that can fail quietly is worse than no check.

## The Honest Ending

The campaign was caught, the planted history was cleaned, and the watchdog now runs whether or not anyone remembers it exists — which is the entire point of a watchdog. Nothing here required exotic skills. It required taking seriously one uncomfortable question:

> *If someone already has the keys to everything I own, what is left that they **cannot** touch?*

Guardian is my answer to that question. It's not inside the vault. That's the feature.

faq.question: What is a supply-chain attack, in simple terms?
faq.answer: Instead of attacking your computer directly, the attacker slips harmful code into something you already trust — a library you install, a tool you use, or your own repository. The damage arrives disguised as part of your normal workflow, which is why ordinary warnings don't fire.

faq.question: Why can't the protection just live inside the repository?
faq.answer: Because anything stored inside a repository — workflows, scripts, settings — can be edited or deleted by whoever holds the repository's write access. The same stolen credential that let the attacker plant code could also switch off a guard stored next to it. That is why Guardian runs from a separate place with read-only access.

faq.question: What happens when Guardian finds something?
faq.answer: It files a GitHub issue so the finding is tracked and deduplicated, and sends a Telegram alert to a private group naming the actual repositories affected. Repo names in public issues are masked with derived codes; the real names only appear in the private alert.
